newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria jails Islamist leader blamed for conflict.
newsitem.headline: Algeria jails Islamist leader blamed for conflict.

text.p: Abdelkader Hachani, once-powerful leader of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), returned to jail to begin a five-year sentence after an Algerian court was told he bore the entire blame for the country's bloody conflict.

A tightly guarded Algiers criminal court, holding a one-day trial after the Islamist leader had been held without trial for more than five years, sentenced him to exactly half the 10 years demanded by the state prosecutor.
He was also stripped of his civil rights for three years, the official Algerian news agency reported.

Hachani, who led the FIS to a landslide victory in Algeria's first mutli-party general election -- only to see it vanish as the authorities in January 1992 scrapped the poll -- heard the state prosecutor tell the court he bore "entire responsibility for the events through which Algeria has lived".
About 60,000 people have been killed in violence that erupted shortly after the ballot was scrapped. Much of the country of 29 million still lives in the shadow of bloodshed.
Hachani was charged with trying to undermine state security just after the December 1991 first round of the election was cancelled.
The charges arose from a statement in his name which appeared in Al Khabar newspaper, urging Algerian soldiers to disobey their officers and not to strike at Islamist activists.

The Defence Ministry accused him of "launching an appeal for rebellion in the army" and on January 22, 1992 he was arrested. He has been held since in Serkadji high security prison near the Casbah in old Algiers.
On Monday, the prosecutor said the Hachani affair should be "put in the context of the epoch" -- the emotion-charged days of the FIS sweep towards power.
Hachani told the judges: "The aim of the appeal was to avoid confrontation and involvement of the ANP (army) in political struggles."
APS said Hachani, now aged about 40, was questioned at length by the judge, to whom he declared he had "always worked within the law" while he headed the FIS.

The court president told Hachani: "The appeal was addressed to members of the ANP and not its command, which implies inciting disobedience and a denial of the public authorities' right to preserve public order in the event of trouble."
Late on Monday, the prosecutor-general asked the court to jail Hachani, a former oil engineer, for 10 years with loss of civil rights.
He was defended by a legal team headed by Ali Yahia Abdennour, leader of an independent Algerian human rights group, and Mustapha Bouchachi.
In London, the human rights group Amnesty International said it had been refused permission by Algerian authorities to send observers to the trial.

Viewed as a relative moderate who had urged FIS activists to avoid violence, Hachani in 1992 termed the cancellation of the poll "a coup d'etat against the Islamic state" which the FIS planned for the North African country.
His party had won 188 of the 232 seats decided outright in the first round.
Along with the former FIS leader, three journalists from Al Khabar were tried but acquitted of publishing "erroneous and tendentious information likely to harm national interest and national unity."
The prosecutor had asked for four years' imprisonment for the journalists, Al Khabar's director, editor and deputy editor.

Algeria last month held the first multi-party general election since the 1992 poll cancellation. Radical Islamists were barred but two moderate Islamist parties were allowed to take part. They won a total of 103 seats in the 380-seat National Assembly.
